opus-5.5.text:
I think finite input-output examples play a really interesting, almost complementary role. They aren't proofs, and that's the whole point of formal verification: a test suite, no matter how large, only checks a finite slice of an infinite input space, while a formal proof says the property holds for *every* input. So in a strict sense, examples can never replace verification.

But in practice they're enormously useful, in a few ways.

First, they're how humans actually communicate intent. When someone writes a specification, it's very easy to get the spec subtly wrong. You prove your sorting function correct, then realize your spec only said the output is sorted and forgot to say it's a permutation of the input. Concrete examples are a sanity check on the specification itself. If your formal spec rejects an example you know should pass, or accepts one that clearly shouldn't, you've found a bug in the spec, not the code. So examples help you verify the verifier, in a sense.

Second, they're a cheap filter. Proving things is expensive, whether it's a human or an AI system searching for a proof. If a candidate program fails on a simple input, there's no point trying to prove it correct. Running examples first lets you throw away wrong candidates quickly and spend proof effort only on the promising ones. That matters a lot when you're generating many candidates with a model.

Third, from an AI perspective, examples are a training signal and a bridge. Much of today's code-generation progress came from unit-test-based rewards, which are noisy and gameable. Models learn to special-case the tests. Formal verification closes that loophole because you can't hard-code your way past a proof. I see examples as the on-ramp: they give dense, easy feedback early, and formal proofs give the final, unforgeable guarantee.

So my view is: examples tell you *what* you mean, proofs tell you that you *got* it. You want both. The mistake is treating passing tests as if it were correctness. The opportunity is using tests to make specifications better and proof search cheaper.

r001.rationale: The response says examples can sanity-check and improve a specification, but does not state that they help turn an informal programming task description into a formal specification.

r002.rationale: The response says to run examples first and discard candidates that fail before spending effort proving them, describing a verification signal available before proof.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that finite examples play a surprisingly important role, but it's a different role from what people usually assume.

The textbook framing is that testing and verification are opposites. Tests show the presence of bugs, never their absence, and a proof shows the absence. So if you have a proof, why would you ever care about examples? But in practice, when we're actually getting a program verified, examples are doing work at almost every stage.

The first place is specification. Formal verification is only as good as the spec you write, and writing a spec is genuinely hard. People get the quantifiers wrong, they forget edge cases, they write something that's trivially satisfiable. Input-output examples are the cheapest sanity check you have. If I write a spec for a sorting function and then I can't even show that sorting the list three, one, two gives one, two, three under my spec, I've made a mistake somewhere. Examples ground the spec in something concrete before you spend hours trying to prove it.

The second place is in the search for a proof itself. When we think about automated or AI-assisted theorem proving, you're essentially navigating a huge space of possible proof steps, lemmas, invariants. Examples are a very fast way to prune that space. If I'm guessing a loop invariant, I can check it against a handful of concrete traces in milliseconds before I ever hand it to a solver. A lot of what makes modern systems practical is this interplay: cheap falsification by examples, then expensive confirmation by proof. You only pay for the proof on candidates that have survived the examples.

And the third place is more about trust and communication. A proof certificate is checkable, but it's not very legible to a human. If I'm handing a verified component to an engineer who doesn't read Lean or Coq, a small set of worked examples is how they build intuition that the spec actually says what they think it says. The proof guarantees the program meets the spec; the examples help a person believe the spec is the right one.

Where I'd push back is on the idea that enough examples can substitute for the proof. They can't, especially for the kinds of properties we care most about, like security properties or behavior on adversarial inputs, where the interesting cases are precisely the ones no one thought to write down. So I'd put it this way: examples are the scaffolding, and the proof is the building. You don't live in the scaffolding, but you'd have a very hard time putting the building up without it.

r001.rationale: The response says examples are a sanity check while writing a specification and help ground it in concrete behavior, illustrated with a sorting example.

r002.rationale: The response says examples can check candidate invariants and prune proof-search options before involving a solver or completing the proof.

astra-6.text:
I see finite input-output examples as useful evidence, but generally not as a proof of correctness. They can help you understand the intended behavior, catch bugs, and formulate a specification. But many different programs can agree on those examples and behave differently on an input you haven’t tried.

Formal verification asks whether the program satisfies a precise specification for every input covered by its assumptions. Examples can guide that process—for instance, a counterexample can reveal that either the program or the specification needs to change. If the input domain is finite and you check it exhaustively, that can establish correctness for that domain. Otherwise, examples support the proof; they don’t replace it.

r001.rationale: It says examples can help understand intended behavior and formulate a specification, directly covering their use in defining a formal specification for an informally described task.

r002.rationale: It describes examples as useful evidence that can catch bugs and guide verification, so they provide a signal before a proof is established.

sol-6.1.text: Finite input-output examples are useful for building intuition and catching mistakes, but they generally aren’t a proof of correctness. A program can pass every example you’ve tried and still fail on an input you haven’t considered. In formal verification, the goal is to show that the program satisfies a precise specification for every input covered by its assumptions. Examples can help you formulate that specification, and counterexamples can help you refine the program or the specification when a proof fails. If the input domain is finite and you check it exhaustively, that’s a different situation—but a handful of examples alone doesn’t establish the general claim.

r001.rationale: It says examples can help formulate a specification, but does not connect this to an informally described programming task.

r002.rationale: It describes examples as useful for catching mistakes while clarifying that they do not prove correctness, communicating their value as a preliminary verification signal.
